text: Two horses climbed the mountain together, matched in stride, neither pulling ahead nor falling back. Where the track levels near the farmhouse a rowan stands alone, leaning into the wind that comes off the ridge, bending but never all the way, holding the ground it has held for years. The horses graze in its lean shadow, breathing hard from the climb. Beyond the tree the lava field opens, and a crack runs black across it, too wide to step over. The horses stop at its edge, Anna, and the ground on the far side is the same ground you stand on now. To reach it there is only the jump, or the turning back.

The root pushed through the stones the hard way, splitting what would not move, until it found the water beneath. Now you come in out of the cold and the stove is already lit, the warmth reaching you before you have taken off your coat, and the house is not empty. What forced its way down through the stone is what feeds this fire tonight. Bank it with ash before you sleep and the embers hold their heat until morning. Keep the flame low and steady, and it will still be there when the grey light comes and you need it again. Nothing that reached the water burns out in a single night.

The keys to the old house lay in your palm long after you had gone, Anna, warm from being held and going nowhere. Now you wake in a different room, and the light on the wall has already shifted while you slept, no hand at the shutter, no reason you can point to. Something has turned that will not turn back. Outside, the birch by the wall has put out its first green while the ground beneath it stays cold and slow to give. Keep on as you are, and the leaves come early whether or not the earth is ready to hold them. You stand at the window with the old keys still in one hand and the new light on the other.

You gave your word once and held to it long past the hour sleep would have taken you, the lamp burning low while the promise stayed whole. That kept word sits in you now like a seed under dark soil, nothing showing at the surface yet, though something has already begun to swell against its own husk. What was paid out in wakefulness has not been lost; it has gone down into the ground where roots take hold. Walk on as you are and what was buried breaks the soil and stands, no longer still but moving, ready to be spent, traded, carried out into the open air. The cost of the sleepless night becomes the herd that grazes the hillside in daylight.

The shore took as much as it gave, each wave drawing back what it had just laid down on the sand. Above the tideline the old turf wall your forefathers raised is sinking now, its stones going green and settling back into the ground that first gave them up. What the sea does in a breath, the wall does across long years, and both are letting go. Up on the slope the sheepdog lies still, its eyes moving over the whole flock, the falling wall, the working shore. Keep walking the way you walk now, and you come to stand where that dog stands, high enough to watch the giving and the losing at once. You are on the slope above the wall, with the sea below and the flock spread out around you.

You wake, and the light in the room has already changed from what you fell asleep in, the walls holding a colour that came from somewhere older than this morning. It is that hour when the dark has thinned but the sun has not yet cleared the ridge, and everything in the room stands half-seen, edges softening into their daytime shapes. Nothing here is fixed yet, and the light is still deciding what it will show you. If you keep lying there, the room will fill slowly, the way it always does, and each thing will take on its full colour in its own time. Do you rise into the light while it is still gathering, or wait until the whole room is plain?

Someone walked this hillside before you, and the track they wore into the grass still holds the shape of their steady climbing. Now the path winds on along the slope of its own accord, taking the easy line the land allows, following the ground rather than fighting it. Your feet find the worn dip in the turf without your looking down. Keep walking as you walk now and the track will bring you over the shoulder of the hill, where the ground opens and the low sun lies flat across the valley. The way was there before you reached it, and it goes on past where you can see.

The thorn hedge had already grown thick across the path long before you came to it, and nothing passed through it without leaving something behind on the barbs. Just past the hedge the lagoon lies still, and your face gathers on its surface, trembling at every breath of wind that finds its way through the thorns. The water holds you whole one moment and scatters you the next, and neither reflection is more true than the other. On the far bank the one who walks with you waits at the same pace you keep, asking nothing, ready to cross when the water goes still. If you stay bent over the lagoon watching your own face break and reform, how long will the one on the other side keep waiting without a word?

Long before you reached the door, Anna, someone had already set the light in the window and drawn the curtain back so it would carry into the dark. That light was placed for you, not earned, and it burned steady through hours no one counted. Now you stand out in the yard where the light falls, not yet inside, the frost of your own breath hanging in the still air. Nothing moves toward the door yet, and the light waits without hurry, as it has waited all along. Keep walking as you are and the last dark thins to grey at the edge of the sky, and the window light and the coming morning meet on the same threshold. You cross into a room already lit.

The rowan by the farmhouse grew tall in years of long light, and the sun found it early each morning through the whole warm season. Now the wind moves through its leaves and they turn one after another, carrying a low sound down the slope. Something is being said in that rustle, and it does not need to be loud to reach you. The tree stands alone against the open sky and never bends all the way, though the same gusts have leaned on it for years. Keep standing where it stands and you will bow but not break, and each hard wind that passes leaves the wood a little older and no less rooted. The rowan holds its ground by the door, as it has, as it does.

The rowan by the farmhouse has weathered many winters, and it stands rooted through all of them, never bending all the way down. Now the ground below it drops toward the glacial river running grey and fast, and the horse steps into that grey water where no crossing shows, feeling the ford out one hoof at a time. You are on its back, Anna, holding the reins while it reads what your eyes cannot. On the far bank the earth looks bare, but a bulb is packed tight beneath it, working in the dark long before anything green breaks the surface. Do you wait on this shore until the water shows its bottom, or do you let the horse carry you across to the ground where that seed is already turning?

The thorn hedge grew close along the old path, and nothing passed it without leaving something torn behind on the barbs. That toll was paid long before you came to the gap. Now you stand at the one narrow place where the branches thin, Anna, watching how the thorns catch the light and reading which are dead wood and which still hold. Your hand is out but not yet through. Keep to this crossing and there is another on the far side, already saddled, standing quiet in the gap you have not yet made. Which thorn are you unwilling to let take its price?

The yew at the river's edge has held its ground through every flood, its roots gripping the black bank while the grey water tore past. It bent to the current long ago and did not go under. Now the horse walks into that same grey water, sure of its footing where your eyes find only churn and silt, and you sit its back with the reins loose. It reads the ford through its own legs, and you are learning to let it. On the far bank the ground is soft and dark, holding what the melt has laid down there, unbroken and waiting. If you keep to the horse's line, where does the crossing set you down — and would you cross at all if you had to see every stone first?

Something sank to the bottom of the lagoon a long while back, and there it has stayed, half-buried in the silt, its shape gone soft under the water. You sit at the table above it now, and the coffee has gone cold in the cup while you watch the surface for a sign of it. Nothing rises, and the water holds flat and still, and still you wait. Then the hail comes down hard across the June field and hammers the lagoon into a thousand broken circles, and when it stops the surface is churned enough that what lay hidden may finally show. How long will you sit over still water waiting for what only rough weather will bring up?

The letter came to your table already sealed, Anna, its words set down by a hand you cannot see and cannot call back. Now it lies there in the still air, and your own hand rests near it without breaking the seal. Nothing turns while the envelope stays closed, and you are the one holding that quiet. Walk on as you are and the seal breaks on its own, the paper opening to whatever was written whether you are ready or not. The words scatter across the table like hail on stone, and what stands afterward is not what stood before.

Long before you noticed, the water moved beneath the ground you stand on, dark and patient under the surface. It found its own way through the earth, needing no permission and leaving no mark you could point to. Now the swell rises far enough to reach your feet, a slow pressure passing between the ground and you, taken up as much as given. What comes toward you and what you return to it move by the same weight, neither one ahead of the other. Keep standing where you are and the water breaks the surface into daylight, plain and warm on the stones. The ground gives up what it carried, and the light lies open on it.

You woke sometime in the night, and by the time your eyes opened the dark had already thinned to grey at the window. Now the first real light comes over the sill and lies across the floor, and it warms the boards where it touches, Anna, spreading wider by the minute. The room you knew in the dark is the same room, only now you can see the whole of it. The light does not stay on the floor alone; it reaches the far wall where another window waits, and what enters here passes through and on. You are sitting in the risen light, the whole room open around you.

The lava field lies quiet now, black rock that once ran molten, and the moss has closed over it like a slow green skin. At its edge a thorn hedge has grown up over the years, and there is a way through it, but the hedge takes something from everything that passes — a thread of wool, a strip of skin, a moment's blood. Past the thorns a single root has found the one crack in the stone and pushes down through it, splitting the rock a hair's width at a time, driving toward the water it cannot yet reach. It does not hurry and it does not stop, and the stone gives only because the root will not. Would you keep pressing where the way costs you, if no one told you the water was there?

Long before you came to the bank, the seed lay whole in the dark soil, holding everything it would ever be and giving nothing away yet. Now the line runs down off your finger into black water, and where it goes below the surface no eye can follow. The water gives back no shape, no weight, nothing you can name from up here. If you keep still and keep watching, the first word will come up the line as a small tug, faint against your hand. You will feel it before you understand it, Anna. You are standing on the bank with the line in the water, waiting for what has not spoken yet.

The sheep-track was already cut into the hillside long before this morning, worn smooth by feet that knew the way down to water and up to grazing. The rowan stands where the track passes the farmhouse, Anna, leaning with the years of wind but never all the way over, its roots holding the same ground through every winter that came for it. And the dog lies a little apart on the rise, where the whole flock stays inside its sight, watching the track and the tree and the scattered grey backs on the slope. If the walking stays as it is, the track keeps its shape and the watch keeps its place. The rowan does not need to move to be held. The hillside carries all three without a sound.

The grain was cut in its own time, threshed and ground and set to rise through the long night, none of it hurried. Now the bread comes hot from the oven, more than one pair of hands could eat, the warmth of it moving out across the whole table. If you keep breaking the loaf the way you break it now, the crust will shatter and the crumb scatter wide, and what falls to the boards feeds a different mouth than yours. The plates come away clean either way. When the last of it is gone from the board, who is still sitting there beside you?

The wood came to the bench knotted and hard, and the blade had to be worked against the grain before it gave anything at all. There was no easy cut in it. Now the shavings curl away clean under the lamp, thin and pale, falling in a soft heap at your feet, and the shape under your hands is finally the one you meant. The work sits easy in the light. Keep the blade moving as it moves now and the single lamp will show you more of the grain than you thought was there, each pass reading what the last one opened. What will you make once you can see the whole of it?

The line ran down into dark water and nothing had touched it yet, the surface holding still over everything it had not begun to reveal. Now the water rises overnight and swells past its own edge, carrying off whatever stood too close to the bank while it slept. What was smooth is breaking, and the loosened silt clouds the depth you could see into before. When the flood settles and the water goes still again, your reflection will sit on the surface of the lagoon, trembling at the least breath of wind. Walk on as you are and the face looking back stays that easily disturbed. When the next gust comes across the water, whose outline are you watching break apart?

The words came down the line and settled, Anna, the thing spoken once and now part of the ground you stand on. By the farmhouse the rowan holds against the wind off the water, leaning but never going all the way over, roots deeper than the leaning shows. It has stood through more than this and it stands still. And along the track past it, someone keeps your pace without needing to be asked, boot beside boot on the same wet stones. If the two of you walk on like this, toward the shore or back toward the house — which way do the tracks lead when you look down at them?

The sheep-track was worn into the hillside long before you came to it, laid down hoof by hoof, each step following the fall of the land. Where the slope steepens the track holds, Anna, cut deep into the turf where a hundred crossings held it against the rain that would have washed a straighter line away. It bends where the ground gives it no other choice, and stays a path all the same. Ahead the track keeps to the high ground, above the boggy hollow, close under the ridge where the wind breaks. You are walking the line the hillside itself would choose.

The shore has always taken and given in the same breath, the water carrying a smooth stone to your feet and drawing the old one back into itself. What it laid down there was fairly traded, one hand open as the other. Now the tide works at what has sat highest on the sand the longest, loosening the driftwood and the shells you thought would stay, turning some of it back to the grey water. What holds fast holds because the sea has let it. Keep walking the tideline as you are and the water stays at your ankles, close enough to reach you, never rising past what you can stand in. You are standing on wet sand where the wave has just gone out, and the next one is still gathering.

The thorn hedge grew wild for years before you came to it, Anna, its wood thickened and its spines set hard by every season it stood. Now you are at the one gap in it, close enough to feel the thorns catch as you press in, and the hedge lets nothing through without taking its price in skin. There is a way past, but it runs narrow between the barbs, and you cannot move fast here. Keep on as you are and the thorns will mark you where they must, one snag at a time, each pull holding you to the slow pace the hedge demands. The far side is not gained by force, only by the crossing itself. What comes through comes through torn, and standing.

A word was spoken on the trail behind you, quiet enough that only you heard it, and it set the direction of the walking. Now the path climbs where the old yew holds the slope, its roots gripping the same ground through every season it has outlasted. You are still on your feet where the ground has asked much of them. Keep to this pace and the one who walks beside you keeps it too, matching each step without a word between you. Neither of you falls behind, neither pulls ahead. The trail goes on, and two sets of tracks run side by side across it.

The dog took its place at the top of the field where the whole flock lay within its sight, and from there nothing could wander off unseen. You sat at the table with your eyes on that same field, and the coffee went cold in the cup while you watched for a sign the sheep were ready to move. The stillness held longer than you meant it to, and still you waited, hands around a cup that had lost its warmth. But the light over the field is already turning, the way night becomes morning without anyone marking the moment it changed. If you keep sitting, the day will come up over the flock whether the cup is warm or cold. When the light has fully turned and the field lies bright before you, will you still be waiting for it to begin?

In the dark shed the forge burned low, and the iron was drawn out and struck into a shape it would keep. Now that shape rides with you along the road by the river, and the road winds ahead and slips out of sight around the next bend. You wake somewhere past that bend, and the light in the room has already changed while you slept. The grey has gone soft at the window and the shed stands quiet, its fire cold, its work carried out into the morning. If you keep to this road, the day will be full up before you have named what it holds. Do you walk on into the light as it is, or stand a while at the window and watch it come?

The hail came hard across the hayfield in June, flattening the young grass in a matter of minutes, and then it was gone before the sky had finished clearing. Now the sun hangs low but never sets over that same field, warming the bruised stalks through the whole long night, and the grass begins to lift again in the endless light. By the south wall the rhubarb noses up through soil the hail had chilled, broad leaves unfurling toward the standing sun. Keep walking as you walk now, Anna, and the field that was struck will be the field that is cut. The green comes up in the same place the ice fell.

The egg lay whole in the nest through the long dark, warm under feather and down, and nothing of what it held ever showed from the outside. Now a line runs from that nest down into still black water, and the surface holds no ripple yet, nothing has touched it. What waits below is not written on the water. A raven settles on the fencepost at the water's edge and folds its wings, in no hurry. It watches the line, it watches you, and it waits for you to listen, Anna. The bird does not call out; it simply stays until you do.

The sun broke through at last and caught the wet stones along the slope, every one of them shining as if the rain had polished them for this. Now a voice carries up from below, saying the thing that has been slow in coming, and the words land clear in the bright air. This is the moment, Anna, where the light and the voice arrive together on the same steep ground. Down through the loose scree a single root runs deep, holding the stones that would otherwise slide, and if you keep to this footing that root will keep its grip while the rest gives way. Does the ground stay firm because of what holds beneath it, or is the shining slope asking to be crossed while the sun is still on it?

The hayfield was left standing until the grass had taken all it could from the summer, cut only when the time was right and not a day before. Now the heath beyond it grows heavy with bilberries, the ground thick with what has ripened on its own slow schedule, more than one pair of hands could gather. This is the fat middle of the season, Anna, when the picking is good and the baskets fill. But the river at the far edge is rising, swollen overnight, and it is pulling at whatever was set down too close to the bank. What sits near that water will not stay where you left it. The current takes the loose things first.

Before the hail came, the field stood open and unmarked, grass rising green with nothing yet decided over it. Now the hail rakes the hayfield in June, flattening the stalks and drumming the earth, and it is gone before the sky clears. What looks like ruin, Anna, is only the sky passing through, hard and brief. When the last stone of ice has melted into the soil, the grass lifts again, and you are standing in the same field, seeing plainly what the weather could not carry off. The field was always yours to walk; the hail only showed you the ground.

Two horses climbed the mountain track together, matching their pace so neither pulled ahead nor fell behind, and that shared rhythm was already set into the stone of the path. Now the climb steepens and the ground turns to loose scree, where the older, deeper-rooted strength in the pair is what keeps the footing sure. The yew on the ridge above has stood through more of these seasons than either horse has walked, its dark needles green while everything around it thins. Ahead the track narrows to a gap between two standing rocks, a gate barely wide enough for one to pass at a time. Keep this pace and you reach that gap side by side, where the mountain asks which of you goes through first.

You held to your word through the long nights, Anna, when it would have been easier to sleep than to keep watch over what you had promised. Now the grass greens over that ground, and the seed-bed gives back nothing yet to the eye, though something roots below where the keeping went. The field looks bare and the work looks unpaid, but the green is not a lie. Keep walking this way and the sheep come in of their own weight toward evening, drifting to the fold slow and without your hand pulling them. What was paid for in wakefulness gathers now on four legs, unhurried.

The glacial river came down grey and heavy through the night, carrying the loosened snow of the high slopes past the door of the house. Now the door stands open to that running water, and coffee waits on the table for two, one cup poured and one still empty. This is the hour, Anna, when the pouring and the drinking are the same warmth passed between hands. The midnight sun holds the hayfield bright past every bedtime, and by that light the cut grass keeps drying in the field. Keep the door open as it is now, and the light stays long enough to bring the hay in. You are standing in the doorway between the grey water and the bright field, with the second cup still warm.

You woke before you meant to, and the light in the room had already changed while you slept, the grey lifting off the walls without a sound. Now that light does not fade the way it once did, for the sun rides low across the sky at midnight and comes back round without ever leaving. The room stays warm with it, the hours lose their edges. Down at the shore the waves keep working, each one laying something new on the black sand and drawing something else back under. You are standing at the tideline in that endless light, hands open, the water reaching your feet and pulling away again.

The hail came hard and stripped the last dead leaves from the branch, and the wind took what was already loose. What the storm broke off will not be growing back. Now the sun reaches the bare wood and warms it through, and the sap runs where the ice held it still. The light finds the birch first. It leafs out ahead of all the rest, green against a ground still cold and hard. Keep opening at this pace, and you stand in leaf while the forest around you is bare — do you know what the frost does to a bud that came too soon?
